title: Is a SOHO unit a good first investment while I work overseas?
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #226 | IS IT A GOOD IDEA BUYING A COMMERCIAL PROPERTY AS A NEW INVESTOR?
excerpt: A first-time buyer in New Zealand is eyeing a SOHO unit under construction in Petaling Jaya. Sean says commercial title has its uses, and to judge it on rent and recent prices, not friends' opinions.

qa.asker: I, a viewer who wrote in by email
qa.context: I has worked in New Zealand for three years, has insurance, emergency savings and retirement contributions in place, and plans to return to Malaysia in three or four years. A bank has put his loan eligibility at about RM1.75 million, but he wants to stay under RM600,000. He likes an under-construction development in the Petaling Jaya area he knows well, near TTDI and One Utama, where his budget only stretches to a SOHO unit. Studio rents nearby are listed at about RM2,100, and he expects RM1,800 to RM1,900.
qa.question: Is the SOHO a good first investment, given its commercial title, the many rival listings and managing it from overseas?
qa.quote: In my opinion, it's not too bad of a deal.
qa.answer: Not a bad deal, as long as the numbers work: compare the rent with the instalment and the price with recent transactions for similar studios. Commercial title doesn't waste his first-home benefits, and owning from abroad works if he pays a property manager and keeps a repair fund.

reasons.title: Commercial title keeps residential slots free
reasons.body: SOHOs and SOFOs fall outside the Housing Development Act, so loans usually stop at about 85%, but developers often offer about 15% off to keep it zero down. They also don't use up the two 90% residential loans, so his next homes can still get them.

reasons.title: Ask who your advisers are
reasons.body: Friends who say studios sell poorly may not invest themselves. Compare studios with and without a direct train link and their distance to major job centres, and check the price isn't well above recent transactions next door.

reasons.title: Investors pay others to manage
reasons.body: Sean once drove to Johor Bahru for a weekend to fix a tenant's curtain, time he says he should have spent earning more. Experienced investors use property managers and rarely meet their tenants.

reasons.title: The deal package changes the cash flow
reasons.body: Paying more upfront means a smaller loan and better cash flow; zero down means topping up maintenance each month; a developer's furnishing package saves cash now but raises the instalment. Which suits him depends on his cash and appetite for risk.

actions: Compare the studio's likely rent with its instalment, and its price with recent transactions for similar units nearby.
Check the loan margin, commercial utility rates and any developer discount before booking.
Line up a property manager or someone you trust near the unit before it's handed over.
Put RM50 to RM100 a month into a separate repair fund for breakdowns and leaks.
Keep researching median prices so you can act quickly when a good deal is offered.
qa.caveat: Sean couldn't say whether the price was good without knowing the channel and terms: buying from the developer, a subsale, a bulk purchase or a contact can change the entry price a lot. He notes that housing rules, such as short-stay bans, can change quickly.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #226. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in October 2023. The viewer mentions taking classes with FAR Capital, a property investment club Sean is a client of.
